meetings.headline: Capital Planning Committee unanimously adopted a tentative order-of-merit ranking of 22 FY27 capital requests
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reviewed members' individual rankings of 22 FY27 capital requests, resolved several ranking ties (including flipping the order of a DPW dump truck and an IT network upgrade), and discussed funding constraints given roughly $3.3 million in requests against a typical $1-1.5 million annual funding capacity. The committee voted unanimously to adopt the resulting order-of-merit list as a tentative recommendation, to be revisited once the town manager's financial picture is clearer, and tentatively scheduled its next meeting for January 28; it also discussed unused ClearGov budgeting software costing about $20,000 a year and outyear capital request planning.

budget_items.topic: Total FY27 capital requests vs. likely funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted requests total roughly $3.3 million while the town typically funds between $1 million and $1.5 million a year from raise-and-appropriate, non-expended capital, or free cash.

A member described a DPW business case showing savings from buying a six-wheel dump truck versus contracting the work, at a cost noted in captions; the town currently has six of seven trucks of that class after recent ARPA investment.

budget_items.topic: Relative sizes of dump truck vs. IT/network items
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair contrasted a large dump truck cost against a much smaller IT activity center network upgrade and school items to illustrate how a funding cutline could reorder priorities.
A member said the network upgrade items seemed cobbled together just to clear a stated capital threshold and said he didn't want to reward that.

A member argued that funding design money alone, rather than full projects, could let the town scope larger items before committing, citing a small design spend as an example of avoiding a bigger unnecessary project.
The town manager said the ClearGov software, currently unused, costs about the figure heard annually and she has not yet decided whether to pause or terminate it.
The town manager said a ballpark free cash number should be available roughly a week before the January 31st closing, accurate to within the figure heard.

what_happened.line: The committee voted unanimously to adopt a tentative order-of-merit ranking of the 22 FY27 capital requests.
The ranking is provisional because requests add up to far more than the town's typical yearly funding capacity from raise-and-appropriate, non-expended capital, or free cash.
Members resolved several ranking ties by discussion, including flipping the order of a DPW dump truck and an IT network upgrade.
The committee plans to revisit the ranking once the town manager's financial picture is clearer.
The next meeting was tentatively set for January 28, pending confirmation once free cash figures are known.

why_it_matters: This ranking shapes which capital purchases -- vehicles, IT upgrades, building repairs -- the town manager and town meeting are likely to fund first next year.
Because requests exceed what the town typically funds in a year, items near the bottom of this list may wait, get scaled to design-only funding, or be cut.
The order is explicitly tentative and tied to the free cash certification, so it can still change before it reaches a town meeting warrant.

No formal votes were taken on funding besides procedural adjournment; the committee agreed to submit written follow-up questions on the DPW plan and discussed how to weigh the special purpose stabilization fund, possible debt exclusions, and a new state zero-emission vehicle mandate against future requests.

budget_items.what_was_said: Chief proposed replacing the 36-year-old light/medium brush truck, which has had repeated breakdowns; an assistance-to-firefighters federal grant was applied for but is almost certainly not awarded due to the federal shutdown.

budget_items.topic: AFG grant match figures for engine 2 and squad/brush truck
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief described the 80/20 federal match structure and what the town's share would have been for engine 2 versus the larger brush truck grant that was not pursued this cycle.
Chief proposed replacing the 2019 ambulance based on 5%-per-year escalation off the 2023 purchase price, with the retired unit kept as a mechanical spare rather than adding a vehicle to the fleet.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Car One (chief's vehicle), pushed to FY28/FY30
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief recommended delaying replacement of his own vehicle a year, noting good mileage and leaving the decision on vehicle type to his successor.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Squad 3 / heavy rescue pumper, moved to FY29
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief moved this big-ticket heavy rescue/pumper replacement out because engine 2 was the higher priority this year; a rough quote was given based on the vehicle as currently equipped, though new lighter equipment (battery tools) may lower the eventual cost.
Chief proposed spacing replacement of the first paramedic-era cardiac monitors over two fiscal years as they reach the 10-year mark, based on 5%-per-year pricing.
Planned replacement continuing the three-vehicle ambulance rotation, cost estimated on a 5%-per-year escalation from the prior purchase.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Heavy-duty brush truck replacement, FY33
budget_items.what_was_said: This AFG-grant-funded truck would be about 30 years old at replacement; chief suggested a possible future swap to a small tanker given town areas without hydrants.
Mutual-aid engine planned for replacement at a 20-year lifespan, cost based on 5%-per-year escalation from the prior engine purchase.
Another planned ambulance replacement on the 5%-per-year escalation model; committee members remarked on how high the projected price has become.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility consultant work, warrant article
budget_items.what_was_said: A special town meeting warrant article would transfer old capital funds to finish consultant work needed before a storm water utility option could be presented to voters at town meeting.

DPW requested funds to complete the bridge project after the original contractor failed to follow through; existing grant and FY22 capital funds cover part of the anticipated construction cost, with more needed for engineering and construction.
DPW compared the cost of renting a loader for the winter versus purchasing, finding purchase cheaper over a 15-year life; last winter's four-month rental was costly.

budget_items.topic: DPW: six-wheel dump truck / salt spreader replacements
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW described replacing aging snow/salt trucks, noting the chassis is a fraction of the cost and the upfitting (plow, dump, spreader) is the larger expense; goal is seven trucks for seven snow routes.

budget_items.topic: DPW: one-ton dump truck replacement schedule
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW obtained multiple quotes for routine one-ton truck replacements and requested funding on the high end of the quoted range to buffer against future price increases.

budget_items.topic: DPW: New West Townsend Road drainage design consultant
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW requested funds to design fixes for roughly eleven undocumented, deteriorating drainage pipe locations along the road; design costs would let construction be phased.
A failing 72-inch pipe under Goodridge Street needs replacement; because of the stream width the project may effectively become a small bridge, raising the cost.

DPW requested design funds to replace the aging, damaged salt shed with a fabric-style structure, also enabling anti-icing liquid infrastructure and reduced salt spillage near the municipal water supply.
Two consultants gave rough cost estimates for engineering an anti-icing liquid system (storage tanks, saddle tanks, spray bars) to reduce salt use.
A member reported the fund balance as of annual town meeting, noting the town cannot expect to add to it soon and asking the committee to weigh which size of project should draw on it.
A member flagged that the track and field project would likely require regular borrowing with a debt service on the order described, over a term no longer than the turf's expected life.

transfers.description: Old capital funds transferred to fund remaining storm-water-utility consultant work, via special town meeting warrant article

decisions.decision: Chair accepted the finance committee's proposal to have a member (Jean Russell) sit in remotely on capital planning meetings while the finance committee chair is traveling.
Chair will build a consolidated spreadsheet covering FY27 requests and out-year requests for a broader prioritization discussion in December or January.
Rather than discuss DPW's full multi-year plan live, the committee will submit written questions (directly or through the chair) to be consolidated and read out at a future meeting.
Chair will share a soft/electronic copy of the annotated draft fiscal policy document and send it to the town manager for review, with the committee to bring back thoughts afterward.

budget_items.topic: Middle high school projector replacement, FY31

meetings.headline: Capital Planning re-elected its officers and began FY27 planning, tabling fiscal-policy threshold changes.
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reorganized for the year, re-electing its chair, vice chair, and clerk, then laid out its FY27 capital planning timeline: department submissions due by end of September, committee review meetings in October and November, and a final ranked list to the town manager by early December. Members reviewed a draft fiscal-policy document (proposed changes to the capital-item dollar threshold and useful-life standard), discussed grant funding uncertainty, gave initial feedback to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire, and approved prior minutes; no capital-plan figures were finalized at this meeting.

votes.motion: Nominate Rob Bowen as vice chair

budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted last year's plan funded a large number of smaller projects, an approach the committee will not have the luxury of repeating.
A member warned that a modest early-year capital list can balloon by year five as departments add speculative items.
A member argued Brooks House projects should be purged from the multi-year plan, calling a large expenditure there unwise.
A member suggested plugging estimated placeholder numbers for known-but-undesigned future work like bridge repairs, even without a specific project identified.

budget_items.topic: Capital item dollar threshold and useful life
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager reviewed a DLS best-practice recommendation to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and questioned whether minimum useful life should move from three to five years.
A member recalled the committee last raised the threshold a couple of years ago somewhat arbitrarily rather than through rigorous analysis.
A member said that aside from a federal grant for fire apparatus, departments generally have little grant funding available for routine, recurring capital needs.
A member said state grant funding is increasingly available for culverts, stormwater and hazard mitigation work, even as federal grant money for the same purposes disappears.
The town manager explained the draft fiscal policy document originated from a community-compact best-practices grant the prior town manager obtained with the state Division of Local Services.
The town manager said the town is already paying for the Clear Gov platform and wants to use it, but does not want it to become a burden on department heads.
A member cited a rough total figure discussed for a Turkey Hill renovation project, noting any significant work there would trigger major building-code thresholds.
A member noted the committee spent ARPA money last year on a consultant study comparing rebuilding versus renovating Turkey Hill, and said he disagreed with the consultants' conclusions.
The town manager said the draft fiscal policy would add a requirement that the committee make a financing recommendation in certain borrowing situations.
A member argued the capital plan should weigh projects against available funding sources, borrowing capacity and free cash, not simply present a ranked list of projects.

decisions.decision: The committee will pursue both its annual prioritized capital list for the town manager and a longer-term five-year plan with a financial-planning component this year.
Department heads' capital submissions are due before the end of September, with committee vetting to begin in October.
The committee will plan for roughly five meeting nights in October and November to review capital proposals.
Final capital-plan rankings are expected to be finalized and voted at meetings in the first or second week of December.
The committee agreed it is wise to hold additional capital planning meetings during the town's budget process, as done last year.

The committee will take as homework whether to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and lengthen the minimum useful-life standard, possibly carving out police cruisers, ahead of the next meeting.
The committee will not require department heads to complete Clear Gov/Collins scoring this year, leaving evaluation criteria to the committee's own discretion.
The committee agreed to consider holding an additional meeting in late September to finish the fiscal-policy discussion and answer the master plan steering committee's questions.
Members expressed general openness to moving the committee's meeting start time earlier, to accommodate town staff schedules.

minutes.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reorganized for the year, re-electing its chair, vice chair, and clerk, then laid out its FY27 capital planning timeline: department submissions due by end of September, committee review meetings in October and November, and a final ranked list to the town manager by early December. Members reviewed a draft fiscal-policy document (proposed changes to the capital-item dollar threshold and useful-life standard), discussed grant funding uncertainty, gave initial feedback to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire, and approved prior minutes; no capital-plan figures were finalized at this meeting.

what_happened.line: Capital Planning set its FY27 timeline: department capital requests are due by the end of September, with review meetings in October and November.
The committee re-elected its chair, vice chair and clerk for the coming year.
A proposal to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and lengthen the minimum useful-life standard was tabled as homework, not decided.

Raising the dollar threshold or lengthening the useful-life standard would change which purchases count as capital items at all -- a decision the committee left open for its next meeting.

what_happened.line: The Capital Planning Committee took no votes on the revised FY26 capital plan; its only vote was to adjourn, and the December 16th minutes were tabled.
The interim Town Manager's recommended warrant list departs from the committee's own rankings on Town Hall HVAC and windows, the primary school generator and the catch basin truck.
The primary school generator estimate rose, and members said its ranking might have dropped; the interim manager will revisit the plan, including the generator and Town Hall items, the next day.
Decommissioning the central and north wings of TC Passos is estimated to be paid from free cash, which reduces the amount available for capital.
The committee will put a report in the warrant book with no article required, and the chair will schedule a meeting on standardizing request forms.

why_it_matters: The warrant list that goes to Town Meeting may not match the committee's own ranking, so the Town Hall envelope repairs and the school generator are still undecided items that residents could be asked to fund.

Free cash used for the TC Passos decommissioning is not available for capital projects, and a resident warned at public comment that several possible borrowings together could breach the town's borrowing policy limits.
